title: The 30 Papers
blurb: A beginner-shaped route through the 27 readings currently published at 30papers.com, from neural-network foundations to compression and complexity.

source.name: 30papers.com
source.note: 30papers.com describes this as the rumoured reading list Ilya Sutskever gave John Carmack. Its public collection currently contains 27 entries, reconstructed from a list shared by Andrew Carr.

papers.title: CS231n: Convolutional Neural Networks for Visual Recognition

notes.takeaway: Course notes that build convolutional networks from linear classifiers, optimization, and backpropagation through the architectures used for visual recognition.
notes.why: Start here when the notation or training loop in later papers feels compressed. The notes supply the working vocabulary that those papers assume.

papers.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks

notes.takeaway: A character-level recurrent network learns enough local and long-range structure to generate convincing prose, code, and mathematical text from raw sequences.
notes.why: The examples make sequence modeling tangible before the formal papers arrive, including both the surprising capability and the failure modes of recurrent generation.

papers.title: Understanding LSTM Networks

notes.takeaway: A visual account of the LSTM cell, showing how gates regulate what a recurrent network keeps, writes, exposes, and forgets across a sequence.
notes.why: Read it before the sequence papers so their LSTM equations resolve into a mechanism rather than a wall of symbols.

papers.title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks

notes.takeaway: AlexNet combines a large labeled dataset, GPU training, rectified linear units, dropout, and data augmentation to decisively improve ImageNet classification.
notes.why: The paper marks the practical break between hand-engineered vision pipelines and the modern deep-learning recipe of scale, compute, and learned representation.

papers.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

notes.takeaway: Residual blocks learn changes relative to an identity path, making optimization stable enough to train image networks hundreds of layers deep.
notes.why: Skip connections became a durable architectural primitive far beyond vision. This paper shows the optimization problem they were designed to solve.

papers.title: Multi-Scale Context Aggregation by Dilated Convolutions

notes.takeaway: Dilated convolutions enlarge a network's receptive field without reducing spatial resolution, allowing dense predictions to use context at several scales.
notes.why: It is a compact study in changing an operator to preserve information that pooling would discard, a recurring concern in structured prediction.

papers.title: Identity Mappings in Deep Residual Networks

notes.takeaway: Clean identity shortcuts and pre-activation blocks improve information and gradient flow through very deep residual networks.
notes.why: The follow-up explains which part of ResNet matters and why. It rewards reading the original architecture as a hypothesis that can be tested and refined.

papers.title: Recurrent Neural Network Regularization

notes.takeaway: Dropout regularizes large LSTMs when applied to their non-recurrent connections, improving generalization without disrupting the recurrent state transition.
notes.why: The paper separates a useful training intervention from the places where that intervention breaks temporal memory, a practical lesson in respecting architecture.

papers.title: Deep Speech 2: End-to-End Speech Recognition in English and Mandarin

notes.takeaway: A single end-to-end system combines recurrent networks, convolution, CTC training, and large-scale compute for speech recognition in two languages.
notes.why: It shows what changes when a model leaves a benchmark and becomes a production-scale sequence system: data, optimization, latency, and hardware all enter the argument.

papers.title: Order Matters: Sequence to Sequence for Sets

notes.takeaway: Sequence models impose an order even when their inputs or outputs are sets, and the chosen order can materially change what the model learns.
notes.why: The paper exposes a representational mismatch that is easy to ignore: the machinery's sequence bias can leak into a problem whose structure is permutation-invariant.

papers.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate

notes.takeaway: A translation decoder learns a soft alignment over source words at each output step instead of relying on one fixed-length encoded sentence.
notes.why: This is attention before the Transformer: a direct answer to the bottleneck created when an entire source sequence must fit into one vector.

papers.title: Pointer Networks

notes.takeaway: The decoder's attention distribution becomes the output, allowing a network to point to positions in an input whose length varies from example to example.
notes.why: The paper turns attention from an internal weighting mechanism into an interface for structured prediction, extending what a sequence model can name.

papers.title: Attention Is All You Need

notes.takeaway: The Transformer replaces recurrence with multi-head self-attention, positional information, and feed-forward layers that train efficiently in parallel.
notes.why: Most modern language-model architecture starts here. Read it after the earlier attention papers to see which constraints the Transformer removes and which it keeps.

papers.title: The Annotated Transformer

notes.takeaway: A runnable implementation walks through the Transformer line by line, connecting the paper's equations to tensors, masks, optimization, and training code.
notes.why: Use it as the laboratory companion to Attention Is All You Need. The implementation turns architecture diagrams into operations you can inspect.

papers.title: Neural Turing Machines

notes.takeaway: A neural controller learns differentiable read and write operations over an external memory, acquiring simple algorithms from input-output examples.
notes.why: The work asks what changes when memory becomes an addressable component rather than a hidden state, a question still active in agent systems.

papers.title: A Simple Neural Network Module for Relational Reasoning

notes.takeaway: Relation Networks apply a shared function to pairs of object representations, giving a larger system an explicit mechanism for comparing entities.
notes.why: The module is intentionally small. Its value comes from matching the architecture to the structure of relational questions rather than adding undirected depth.

papers.title: Relational Recurrent Neural Networks

notes.takeaway: A recurrent core uses self-attention over a memory matrix so stored items can interact before the next state is produced.
notes.why: It joins two threads in the list, recurrence and relational attention, and tests whether memory works better when its contents can reason over one another.

papers.title: Neural Message Passing for Quantum Chemistry
papers.firstAuthor: Gilmer, Schoenholz, Riley, Vinyals, and Dahl

notes.takeaway: A common message-passing framework unifies several graph neural networks and predicts molecular properties by exchanging information along chemical bonds.
notes.why: The framework makes relational computation concrete on graphs, where the data structure already declares which entities may communicate.

papers.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

notes.takeaway: Language-model loss follows predictable power laws with model size, data, and compute across the measured regime, exposing tradeoffs between those inputs.
notes.why: The paper turns scaling from an intuition into an empirical planning model and helps explain why research strategy moved toward larger training runs.

papers.title: GPipe: Efficient Training of Giant Neural Networks using Pipeline Parallelism

notes.takeaway: Pipeline parallelism partitions a model across accelerators and splits batches into micro-batches so several partitions can work at once.
notes.why: Scaling laws only matter when systems can execute the implied training runs. GPipe shows one mechanism for turning model size into a schedulable workload.

papers.title: Keeping Neural Networks Simple by Minimizing the Description Length of the Weights

notes.takeaway: A network can be regularized by minimizing how many bits are needed to describe its weights while still accounting for the training data.
notes.why: The paper connects generalization to compression early in the history of neural networks and sets up the description-length readings that follow.

papers.title: A Tutorial Introduction to the Minimum Description Length Principle

notes.takeaway: Minimum Description Length chooses the model that gives the shortest combined encoding of the model and the data explained by it.
notes.why: The tutorial supplies the formal language behind the intuition that learning and compression are closely related, without requiring the reader to infer it from fragments.

papers.title: The First Law of Complexodynamics

notes.takeaway: A blog essay asks how to formalize the observation that complexity often rises and later falls as a closed system approaches equilibrium.
notes.why: The question reframes complexity as a trajectory rather than a synonym for entropy, preparing the concrete coffee-automaton model that follows.

papers.title: Quantifying the Rise and Fall of Complexity in Closed Systems: The Coffee Automaton

notes.takeaway: A cellular automaton for mixing coffee and cream tests candidate measures of complexity as a system moves from order through structure to equilibrium.
notes.why: The model gives the previous essay an object you can simulate, measure, and disagree with instead of leaving the complexity claim at the level of metaphor.

papers.title: Kolmogorov Complexity

notes.takeaway: Kolmogorov complexity defines the information in a string by the length of the shortest program that can generate it on a fixed universal machine.
notes.why: This is the formal backbone of algorithmic description length, including the sharp limit that the quantity itself cannot generally be computed.

papers.title: Variational Lossy Autoencoder

notes.takeaway: An autoregressive decoder and variational latent code divide information so the model can choose what to preserve globally and what to reconstruct locally.
notes.why: The paper makes lossy representation a design variable, connecting the abstract compression block to a trainable generative model.

papers.title: Machine Super Intelligence

notes.takeaway: A doctoral thesis develops a formal measure of universal intelligence and studies the behavior and consequences of agents that score highly under it.
notes.why: It closes the path by asking what intelligence means when the definition must range across environments rather than one benchmark or one task family.

sections.label: Build the working vocabulary
sections.summary: Three generous explanations establish the mechanics that the papers will later compress into notation: convolutional networks, recurrent generation, and LSTM memory.
themes: Learn the training loop and architecture vocabulary before reading compressed conference prose.
Use visible behavior to connect recurrent state and gating to what sequence models can produce.

sections.label: Depth becomes trainable
sections.summary: ImageNet scale, residual paths, dilation, and pre-activation trace a compact history of how vision networks became deeper without giving up optimization or resolution.
themes: Data, compute, and regularization establish the modern deep-learning recipe.
Identity paths and receptive fields become explicit architectural choices.

sections.label: Sequences meet the real world
sections.summary: Regularization, speech recognition, and unordered sets test recurrent models against overfitting, production constraints, and data whose structure does not naturally fit a sequence.
themes: Regularize the model without damaging its recurrent memory.
Separate the sequence machinery from the structure of the problem.

sections.label: Attention removes the bottleneck
sections.summary: Alignment begins as a learned look-back for translation, becomes an output pointer, and finally replaces recurrence in the Transformer.
themes: Attention starts as a way around the fixed-vector bottleneck.
The Transformer turns that mechanism into the main computational substrate.

sections.label: Memory becomes an interface
sections.summary: External memory, relation modules, self-attentive recurrent state, and graph message passing make storage and interaction explicit parts of the architecture.
themes: Addressable memory changes what a neural controller can learn to do.
Relational structure guides which representations should interact.

sections.label: Scale becomes predictable
sections.summary: Empirical power laws explain why larger training runs pay, while pipeline parallelism shows how those runs can be divided across hardware.
themes: Model, data, and compute trade against one another in measurable ways.
Systems design determines whether the scaling plan can run.

sections.label: Compression frames the whole field
sections.summary: Description length, algorithmic complexity, lossy representation, and universal intelligence pull the practical arc back toward a harder question: what makes a learned explanation simple?
themes: Compression offers a language for model selection and generalization.
Complexity can rise and fall even while entropy moves in one direction.
Formal intelligence asks how an agent performs across environments, not one benchmark.
